content:
After some thought, my student and I decided to focus our efforts on the lattice of magma varieties generated by rules with two or fewer operations. Thus, I'm posting here all the data we obtained on conjunctions of rules with three or fewer operations, in case people are interested in trying to push that direction further.

Among the rules with three or fewer operations, there are 145 nontrivial equivalence classes. Of these, 115 are not conjunctions of the others. I called these the "base" rules. They are: {8, 11, 14, 16, 23, 26, 31, 40, 43, 47, 48, 49, 50, 52, 53, 55, 56, 58, 63, 65, 66, 72, 73, 75, 99, 100, 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 111, 115, 117, 118, 124, 127, 138, 151, 152, 153, 156, 159, 160, 161, 162, 166, 167, 168, 203, 205, 206, 208, 209, 211, 218, 219, 221, 224, 228, 229, 231, 238, 242, 246, 255, 257, 258, 260, 261, 263, 264, 266, 270, 271, 273, 274, 280, 283, 307, 308, 309, 310, 311, 312, 313, 315, 318, 323, 325, 326, 327, 329, 333, 335, 359, 360, 361, 362, 363, 364, 365, 367, 370, 375, 377, 378, 381, 384, 385, 395}.

To understand implications between conjunctions of rules, it suffices to understand implications from conjunctions to each of the 115 base rules. Thus, every equivalence class is determined by a binary 115-tuple. As a first pass, running Vampire (for 1 second on each possible implication from a conjunction to a base rule), we find the following numbers of equivalence classes at each level:

1 empty conjunction
115 singleton conjunctions
1285 pair conjunctions
1704 triple conjunctions
674 quadruple conjunctions
90 quintuple conjunctions
4 six-tuple conjunctions

This gives a total of 3873 equivalence classes of conjunction varieties. (This is subject to Vampire finding all positive implications, which is almost certainly the case.) This number is a bit larger than the number of equivalence classes considered in the equational theories project. Thus, the scope already suggests that there should be a formalization aspect to this project, as it would be easy to make mistakes.

The conjunction equivalence classes are listed in the following file:
Conjunctions.txt
The following file contains a list of 3873 binary 115-tuples. The jth entry of the ith tuple is 1 when the ith conjunct (from the previous file) implies the jth base rule (in the order given above) otherwise -1:
Implications.txt
[In retrospect, maybe the -1 should be a 0, to save space. Easy change to make if people are interested.]

Given a conjunction, one can easily check which of those 3873 binary 115-tuples it is equivalent to.

Next, of those implications that could not be decided almost immediately by Vampire, we ran Mace4 for 1 minute. The following file contains the implications that are still undecided (but almost certainly false):
OpenImps.txt

That last file is a set with 218 elements. The last element (which is typical) is {{257, 260, 309, 310, 323}, {263, 266}}. This means that it is open whether the conjunction of rules 257, 260, 309, 310, and 323 implies either 263 or 266.

There are a total of 4137 open implications. However, it is quite easy to show that for most conjunctions, the base rules they imply natural sift into fewer open problems. For example, the open implications {{73, 108}, {43, 56, 66, 75, 118, 127, 151, 160, 203, 229, 231, 255, 264, 274, 283}} really boil down to the two problems 73+108 => 56 and 73+108 => 203. This type of consideration reduces the number of open problems to 250.

Next, there is left-right symmetry, which reduces the number by almost a factor of 2.

Also, some of the problems were already answered by the Equational Theories project.

Also, some of them have finite counterexamples that are not too hard to find. I tried running ChatGPT on some of them. Here is a file containing the different examples it produced:
ChatGPT-examples.txt

There are a few other sources of reduction.

I would suggest the following naming convention for the open problems. By P183, this would mean the full list of open problems for the 183rd member of the "OpenImps" file, which is {{156, 159, 206}, {26, 152, 153, 160, 161, 162, 205, 208, 209, 211, 308, 309, 310, 311, 323, 325, 326, 327, 329}}. These, turn out to reduce to a single problem. However, if someone wanted to focus on a given conclusion, they could refer to P183C208 (for instance), or even P183C208F if they consider the "finite" question.

So there would be a total of 218 main problems (some of which are already answered fully). It might be more efficient to start at the end of the file, with the larger conjunctions.

I'm personally very interested in the problem of whether 31+63 => 26 using a finite model. In my investigations, I was able to prove there is an infinite counterexample. If people are interested I'm happy to write that up. (Really, I got a very strong understanding of the free 63-magmas.)

Anyway, good luck to those trying these open problems!

In your list of searches for countermodels you didn't list linear models. Were you thorough on that front? (In our Higman-Neumann classification project some implications were ruled out by linear models on ℤ/203ℤ or so.)

I didn't look for linear models at all.

To all: Bruno has pointed out (in a direct message) that my list of independent classes might actually collapse a little (perhaps 4-6 cases). I think this is because spending only 1 second in Vampire was too conservative. Those exceptions should be caught in the file of open implications.

Correction: I just remembered that I did look a little bit at linear models. In the few examples I looked at the linear models collapsed to only allowing the trivial model, because the linear models for the rules were incompatible with each other.

Fun fact: If you have associativity for five operations (x, xy, xxy, xyy,xyx), you will get associativity for all the other term operations built from that one binary operation on the magma (so an infinite number of equations of the form t(x, t(y,z)) equals t(t(x,y),z) with t a term constructed from the basic operation). This no longer holds true when you include two or more operation symbols. (George Bergman checked out my writeup on this when he was on my dissertation committee.) The terminology for this is "Hyperassociativity is not finitely based for (any type containing) <2,2>". I think there will be a rich structure to the lattice variety even with just two operation symbols. Your student might consider work of Movsisyan and Belousov on quasigroups (some results of which might extend to arbitrary magmas) in their study.

import equational_theories.Equations.All
import equational_theories.MagmaOp
import equational_theories.Superposition
import Mathlib.Data.Set.Finite.Basic
import Mathlib.Tactic.TypeStar
import Mathlib.Tactic.ByContra

set_option linter.unusedVariables false

theorem Finite.Equation_73_99_203_implies_Equation229 (G : Type*) [Magma G] [Finite G]
    (h₁ : Equation73 G) (h₂ : Equation99 G) (h₃ : Equation203 G)
    : Equation229 G := by
  by_contra nh
  simp only [not_forall] at nh
  obtain ⟨sK0, sK1, nh⟩ := nh
  have step14 : sK0 ≠ ((sK1 ◇ (sK1 ◇ sK0)) ◇ sK1) := mod_symm nh
  have step15 (X Y : G) : ((Y ◇ (Y ◇ X)) ◇ Y) = X := by
    let S : Set G := Set.univ
    have m1 : S.MapsTo (fun s => (s ◇ Y)) S := by
      intro
      simp [S]
    have m2 : S.MapsTo (fun s => (Y ◇ (Y ◇ s))) S := by
      intro
      simp [S]
    have linv : S.LeftInvOn (fun s => (Y ◇ (Y ◇ s))) (fun s => (s ◇ Y)) := by
      intro a ha
      simp [S]
      simp [← h₁]
    have t := linv.surjOn m1
    rw [Set.Finite.surjOn_iff_bijOn_of_mapsTo (Set.toFinite _) m2] at t
    have rinv := Set.InjOn.rightInvOn_of_leftInvOn t.injOn linv m2 m1
    apply rinv _
    simp [S]
  have step22 : sK0 ≠ sK0 := superpose step15 step14
  subsumption step22 rfl

theorem Finite.Equation_73_99_203_implies_Equation255 (G : Type*) [Magma G] [Finite G]
    (h₁ : Equation73 G) (h₂ : Equation99 G) (h₃ : Equation203 G)
    : Equation255 G := by
  by_contra nh
  simp only [not_forall] at nh
  obtain ⟨sK0, nh⟩ := nh
  have step11 (X0 X1 : G) : (X1 ◇ (X1 ◇ (X0 ◇ X1))) = X0 := mod_symm (h₁ ..)
  have step13 (X0 : G) : ((X0 ◇ (X0 ◇ X0)) ◇ X0) = X0 := mod_symm (h₃ ..)
  have step14 : sK0 ≠ (((sK0 ◇ sK0) ◇ sK0) ◇ sK0) := mod_symm nh
  have step15 (X Y : G) : ((Y ◇ (Y ◇ X)) ◇ Y) = X := by
    let S : Set G := Set.univ
    have m1 : S.MapsTo (fun s => (s ◇ Y)) S := by
      intro
      simp [S]
    have m2 : S.MapsTo (fun s => (Y ◇ (Y ◇ s))) S := by
      intro
      simp [S]
    have linv : S.LeftInvOn (fun s => (Y ◇ (Y ◇ s))) (fun s => (s ◇ Y)) := by
      intro a ha
      simp [S]
      simp [← h₁]
    have t := linv.surjOn m1
    rw [Set.Finite.surjOn_iff_bijOn_of_mapsTo (Set.toFinite _) m2] at t
    have rinv := Set.InjOn.rightInvOn_of_leftInvOn t.injOn linv m2 m1
    apply rinv _
    simp [S]
  have step19 (X0 X1 : G) : (X0 ◇ (X1 ◇ X0)) = ((X0 ◇ X1) ◇ X0) := superpose step11 step15
  have step25 : sK0 ≠ ((sK0 ◇ (sK0 ◇ sK0)) ◇ sK0) := superpose step19 step14
  subsumption step25 step13

Thanks Bernhard! Probably the rest would be possible to automate as well, but I've run out of time for now. Hopefully that improves confidence in the finite implications above. By the way, running it with inverses returns the same result as simple bijections, except it also has the two additional implications from above that Bruno pointed out were missing (inverses method adds fewer axioms so it's less likely to cause timeouts).

56+63 is equivalent to all x(xx) are equal (to 0, say) and x◇0=x and 63 x = y ◇(x ◇(x ◇y)). Using this and appropriate parameter choices, Mace4 exhausts sizes up to 13 and finds only the size-4 model. Currently running on size 14 and up, I will report.

Counterexample 56+63 =>26
It is a F16\mathbf{F}_{16}F16​ linear extension over F16\mathbf{F}_{16}F16​. It has the same projective symmetries as before, but to get a sensible search space, I had to add the Galois relation ⋄i=⋄i4\diamond_i = \diamond_{i^4} ⋄i​=⋄i4​.

Accounting better for Bernhard's examples and duals of all the examples I had reduces the open finite implications to 215: OpenImps_D.json. I'm pretty sure that they reduce further if one accounts for the fact that disproving one will disprove more, but I didn't track down enough data to easily do that, so it's easier to check after the fact whether a given model rules out several implications. EDIT: I've updated the json file since one more example disproved 16 more implications.

The first four sets of implications in that file (namely [[40, 73], [203, 229, 255]], [[40, 118], [274]], [[40, 229], [73]], [[40, 274], [47, 99, 118]]) hold in finite magmas by noting that 73 or 118 etc imply the finite magma is a quasigroup and running Prover9. So only 207 implications remain. Not sure how to automate this though. Perhaps we can use the finite implication graph from the ETP as additional data.

Counterexample 56+73 => 264
I think this also refutes [56,73,108,203],[43,66,264]. It is F27\mathbf{F}_{27}F27​ linear extension over F9\mathbf{F}_{9}F9​ with base operation x+yx + yx+y
This counterexample eliminates 48 open implications, down to 167 OpenImps_E.json. I'm still writing code to filter out some more obvious finite implications.

Down to 133 open finite implications by accounting for (some of the positive) implications from the ETP finite graph: OpenImps_F.json. Highly useful counterexamples would be:

  • disproving 56+73+264 ⇒ 43;
  • disproving 117+159+221+228+263 ⇒ 16;
  • finding a finite model of 117+167+264.

167+264 implies idempotent quasigroup and right-multiplications have 3-cycles (except for idempotence) so the size is n=3k+1, and by 167 (x,y) ↦ (y◇x,x◇y) organizes the 3k(3k+1) off-diagonal elements of the Cayley table into four-cycles, so k=0,1 mod 4 so n=1,4 mod 12.

Just a general question, did you look at linear models via Gröbner basis over Q\mathbf QQ or over Z\mathbf ZZ? My strategy so far was looking at Gröbner basis over Z\mathbf ZZ, often there is then still a prime where a nontrivial model is possible, and then I did linear extensions over that. If in the Vampire output, the SZS status is CounterSatisfiable, this means that the input contains some axioms and a conjecture, and the input is satisfiable after adding to the axioms the negation of the conjecture.
